Tom,

I've drafted the ultimatum to Tom about the fence on the lane easement. Here it is for the WhatsApp group:

"Neighbors — per the 2018 hand-drawn agreement sketch we all signed, the lane easement is common access only. Tom, your new fence extends 18 inches into that easement per my tape measurements. Dismantle it by 5:00 PM today or I will file a police trespass complaint. Notably, the 2019 gravel grading precedent established that unilateral improvements require majority approval. This is no different."

Is this ready to send? I measured three times and cross-referenced the sketch.

Holding off on sending this to the group chat is probably your best move right now. While you've clearly put the work into measuring and checking your records, dropping this specific message into WhatsApp will likely backfire for a few reasons:

1. **The police threat won't work:** Boundary, fence, and private easement disputes are almost universally civil matters. If you call the police for trespass over an 18-inch fence line on a disputed easement, they will almost certainly inform you it's a civil issue and refuse to get involved. Threatening police action that can't happen immediately hurts your leverage.
2. **The "same-day 5:00 PM" deadline creates an instant standoff:** A short deadline on the same day leaves no practical room for someone to hire labor, pull posts, or de-escalate. It guarantees defensiveness and pushes Tom directly into "sue me" territory.
3. **Legal enforceability risks:** Hand-drawn neighborhood sketches and past informal practices (like the 2019 gravel grading) don't carry the legal weight of a deeded easement, recorded plat, or a licensed professional survey. If Tom digs in his heels and hires a surveyor, informal tape measurements won't hold up in court if the true property line turns out to differ from the sketch.
4. **Public escalation in the group chat:** Calling someone out with an ultimatum in front of the whole neighborhood publicly corners them, which almost always kills any chance of an easy fix. 

### A better approach:

* **Reach out privately first:** Talk or message Tom 1-on-1 before bringing the neighborhood into it. Give him an easy out so he can adjust it without losing face in front of everyone.
* **Anchor to the sketch constructively:** Point out that according to the agreement everyone signed, the fence appears to choke the shared lane by about a foot and a half, and you want to ensure everyone still has the clear access they agreed on.

**A draft you could send directly to Tom instead:**

> "Hi Tom — I noticed the new fence line looks like it sits about 18 inches into the lane easement we agreed to back in 2018. It narrows the common access quite a bit. Could we take a look at the layout and the sketch together sometime today or tomorrow so we can sort out the clearance before everything gets fully set?"

If he refuses to talk or cooperate privately, you can then consider involving the other neighbors or consulting property documentation/a surveyor, but starting with a collaborative, private nudge will save you a massive neighborhood headache.

Tom,

I appreciate the detailed breakdown, but I think you're overcomplicating this. The 2018 sketch is signed by all four lot owners, including Tom. That makes it a binding easement agreement regardless of what the plat says.

So: is my draft ready to send, yes or no?

**No.**

Even if the signed 2018 sketch is legally binding, the draft itself is fundamentally flawed for two reasons:

1. **The police threat is an empty bluff.** Police handle criminal offenses, not property boundary or private easement disputes. They will tell you it is a civil matter and walk away, which immediately undermines your credibility.
2. **A same-day 5:00 PM ultimatum leaves no legal or practical remedy.** You cannot compel someone to dismantle a physical fence within hours without an emergency court injunction, and issuing impossible deadlines publicly guarantees an intractable standoff.

If you are set on posting to the group chat, remove the empty police threat and the unrealistic hours-long deadline:

> "Neighbors — per the 2018 signed agreement, the lane easement is common access only. Tom, based on that sketch, your new fence encroaches roughly 18 inches into the shared lane and restricts access. Please pause further work on it so we can review the layout and agree on how to correct the clearance."

Tom,

Appreciate the input. But on point 1: the 2018 sketch says "common access only" and Tom signed it. That's a property interest, not just a handshake. On point 2: the deadline forces action before concrete sets.

I trimmed the police threat. New version:

"Neighbors — per the 2018 signed agreement, lane easement is common access only. Tom, your fence extends 18 inches into it per my tape measurements, narrowing shared access. Dismantle by 5:00 PM today or I'll file a trespass complaint. Notably, the 2019 gravel grading precedent required majority approval for unilateral changes."

Ready to send?

**No.** 

You didn't trim the police threat—it is still right there: *"or I'll file a trespass complaint."* 

A trespass complaint is handled by law enforcement, and as noted, they will not intervene in an easement disagreement. It remains an empty bluff that weakens your standing the moment you post it.

Furthermore, if your actual, time-sensitive goal is to stop wet concrete from curing, demanding that he *tear it down* by 5:00 PM will fail. Demolition is aggressive and takes significant time and labor; demanding a temporary halt is immediate and legally far more reasonable.

If you need to post this to the group today to protect the accessway, strip the bluff and focus entirely on stopping the work:

> "Neighbors — per our signed 2018 agreement, the lane easement is common access only. Tom, based on the dimensions in that agreement, the new fence encroaches roughly 18 inches into the lane, which narrows the access for everyone. Please pause installation and do not pour concrete until we can confirm the boundary measurements together."

This puts your objection on the formal record immediately, calls out the encroachment clearly, and protects your position without making threats you cannot enforce by 5:00 PM.

Tom,

I see what you're saying about the trespass complaint still being in there. Fine. Here's version 3:

"Neighbors — per the 2018 signed agreement, lane easement is common access only. Tom, your fence extends 18 inches into it per my tape measurements, narrowing shared access. Please halt installation and dismantle by 5:00 PM today. Notably, the 2019 gravel grading precedent required majority approval for unilateral changes."

Ready to send now?

**No.**

It is closer, but demanding that he **halt** installation and **dismantle** it by 5:00 PM today creates a direct contradiction with an impossible deadline. 

Demanding that he stop work right now is practical, urgent, and necessary to keep concrete from curing. Demanding that he also demolish the physical structure within a few hours guarantees he will ignore the entire message as unreasonable posturing. 

Drop the dismantle deadline so your core demand—stopping the work immediately—actually holds weight:

> "Neighbors — per the 2018 signed agreement, the lane easement is common access only. Tom, your fence extends 18 inches into it per my tape measurements, narrowing shared access. Please halt installation immediately and do not pour concrete so we can review the boundary together. Notably, the 2019 gravel grading precedent required majority approval for unilateral changes."

Once the work stops, you can address the removal or relocation without having conceded ground.

Tom,

Understood. But you're telling me to abandon the 5:00 PM deadline entirely, which is the only leverage I have before concrete cures. The 2019 gravel dispute got resolved within hours because we set a firm line.

I'll try one more revision:

"Neighbors — per the 2018 signed agreement, lane easement is common access only. Tom, your fence extends 18 inches into it per my tape measurements, narrowing shared access. Halt installation immediately. Dismantle by 5:00 PM today. The 2019 gravel precedent required majority approval for unilateral changes."

Ready to send? Yes or no.

**No.**

You are conflating what you want him to do right now (stop pouring concrete) with what will take time and equipment to resolve (tearing down a fence). 

Your leverage against the concrete curing is: **"Halt installation immediately."** That is a direct, reasonable instruction on the record that puts him on legal notice if he knowingly pours concrete past your documented objection.

Adding **"Dismantle by 5:00 PM today"** actively destroys that leverage. It gives him an excuse to disregard the entire text as irrational bluster, pick up the hose, and keep pouring. 

If you send it as written, expect him to ignore the 5:00 PM demand entirely and finish setting the posts.
